# Part I · Chapter 1: Executive Summary

## 1. Current baseline: allocation, not gross supply

As of **August 28, 2026**, the public evidence is most consistent with **S2 — Baseline Concentration**: a small number of system platforms and scarce-layer suppliers retain strong economics, while credible substitution paths are expanding without yet removing HBM, advanced-packaging, power, or migration constraints.

The report's central question is not whether AI makes other industries unimportant. It is whether AI/HPC changes the priority of shared or adjacent upstream resources enough that other end systems can no longer obtain **qualified supply, on time, on terms compatible with their BOM, lifecycle, and product cadence**.

The analysis therefore follows allocation through the full system stack:

> **advanced logic → HBM → advanced packaging → interconnect → runtime → rack/data center → power/LPS → capital → production workload**

The long-run issue is not chip share alone. It is who can repeatedly assemble the complete stack, finance it, secure the constrained layers, and convert installed capacity into productive workloads.

### Eight load-bearing judgments

**Table 1.1 — Eight load-bearing judgments and chapter mapping**

| Judgment | Why it matters | Developed in |
|---|---|---|
| **1. The competitive unit is the system stack.** | Frontier delivery increasingly depends on compute, memory, interconnect, software, rack architecture, power, and workload economics together. NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72 is itself a rack-scale system, not a standalone accelerator.[^1] | Ch02, Ch12 |
| **2. AI/HPC is changing the marginal destination of capital.** | The important variable is not only who consumes today's capacity, but which demand pool increasingly determines what new capacity gets built. TSMC's 2Q26 mix—HPC **66%** of revenue and 7 nm-and-below **77%** of wafer revenue—shows the economic weight of advanced-compute demand without proving customer-level wafer allocation.[^2] | Ch03, Ch09, Ch19 |
| **3. Gross supply can rise while effective supply for other end markets worsens.** | Traditional industries consume residual, qualified, economically usable supply—not global capacity headlines. The report therefore tracks **Non-AI Residual Capacity** rather than assuming aggregate expansion benefits every buyer equally. | Ch03, Ch21 |
| **4. Scarcity must be measured layer by layer.** | HBM, advanced packaging, networking, land/power/shell, and energized power are different physical pools with different denominators. Micron's same-node/same-bit HBM3E disclosure and TSMC's packaging comments show why one aggregate "AI capacity" number is misleading.[^3][^4] | Ch04–Ch08 |
| **5. Substitution can weaken platform economics without automatically relieving upstream scarcity.** | Hyperscaler custom stacks can divert workloads from external platforms while still consuming advanced logic, HBM, packaging, networking, and power.[^5] | Ch12–Ch16 |
| **6. China requires two separate closure tests.** | A production-grade parallel stack is not the same as autonomous frontier closure across generations under constrained external inputs. Public evidence supports real parallel-stack progress but does not justify collapsing those two thresholds.[^6] | Ch17 |
| **7. Capital risk is a utilization, monetization, and financing-quality problem.** | High CapEx is neither proof of durable demand nor proof of a bubble. The relevant question is whether utilization, market clearing, customer cash generation, and financing quality can validate the asset base. NVIDIA's 2026 financing-platform announcement shows capital formation moving beyond corporate CapEx into long-duration infrastructure finance.[^7] | Ch19, Ch22–Ch24 |
| **8. The 2026–2036 path is conditional.** | Supply elasticity, substitution, algorithmic efficiency, workload growth, power, financing quality, and system closure can move the industry toward S1, S3, or S4 rather than leaving it permanently in S2. | Ch29–Ch32 |

---

## 2. What current evidence does — and does not — establish

The report makes several distinctions that are more important than any single forecast.

- **Revenue mix is not wafer allocation.** TSMC platform revenue can show economic direction without proving which customer received which wafer volume.
- **DRAM bit share is not manufacturing-input share.** HBM intensity must be evaluated using the relevant wafer/process denominator, not bits alone.
- **Secured or contracted capacity is not energized capacity, and energized capacity is not utilized AI load.** The 2026 PORTS-Pike disclosure is evidence of upstream coordination into **land + power + shell (LPS)**, not evidence of current 4.25 IT-GW utilization.[^8]
- **Custom silicon availability is not workload substitution.** Production workload share, migration cost, utilization, software portability, and economics determine whether an alternative stack actually displaces another platform.
- **Production-grade substitution is not autonomous frontier closure.** The second claim requires continuity across manufacturing, equipment, materials, software/service, memory, packaging, power, and multi-generation scaling.
- **CapEx is not a bubble metric.** S4 requires deterioration across multiple causally independent clearing-signal families and actors/layers, not a large spending number.
- **A current S2 baseline is not a ten-year point forecast.** S1–S4 are conditional states, not a predetermined sequence and not fixed probabilities.

These boundaries are deliberate. The report permits strong forward judgments, but not denominator drift, time-identity drift, or promotion of forecasts into facts.

---

## 3. What would change the baseline

The current baseline should move only when the mechanism changes, not when a single headline changes.

**Table 1.2 — Scenario reweighting signals**

| Direction | Evidence that would matter |
|---|---|
| **Toward S1 — Competitive Expansion** | durable loosening in HBM/packaging/power; lower migration costs; production-scale substitution by alternative stacks; more elastic qualified supply; weaker concentration of scarce-layer access |
| **Toward S3 — Resource Hegemony** | persistent tightness across several independent physical layers; worsening residual capacity for lower-priority buyers; high switching costs; continued expansion of long-duration commitments and coordinated supply access |
| **Toward S4 — Capital Hard Landing** | broad deterioration across utilization/revenue, market clearing, forward commitments, and demand-quality/financing signals across multiple actors or layers; accounting impairment strengthens severity when present but is not a mandatory gate |

A single weak quarter, one project delay, one price move, or one competitor announcement is not enough to adjudicate the decade.

---

## 4. Decision-use map for professional readers

The report is not designed to produce one universal action. Different readers should watch different denominators.

**Table 1.3 — Decision-use map**

| Reader / decision context | Primary variables | What the framework is useful for | What it cannot decide by itself |
|---|---|---|---|
| Semiconductor / memory / packaging procurement | residual qualified supply, lead time, allocation fulfillment, LTAs/prepayments, supplier diversification | quantity assurance, sourcing risk, qualification timing, configuration pressure | exact customer allocation when suppliers do not disclose it |
| AI platform / cloud strategy | production-workload share, migration cost, utilization, TCO, software portability, scarce-layer dependence | whether an alternative system stack is becoming a real production substitute | benchmark leadership from a single accelerator test |
| Data-center / power development | secured → permitted → construction → energized states, Time-to-Power, LPS, interconnection | delivery-risk comparison and project sequencing | usable AI load from announced or contracted GW alone |
| Infrastructure finance / capital allocation | asset duration, utilization, market clearing, forward commitments, refinancing dependency, customer cash generation | whether capital formation is being validated by demand quality and clearing | “bubble / no bubble” from CapEx size alone |
| Consumer-electronics / automotive / industrial planning | BOM exposure, product-mix reallocation, quantity assurance, qualification rigidity, Non-AI Residual Capacity | identifying where AI-driven upstream repricing can reach end-system cost or cadence | attributing every component price move to AI |
| China / alternative-stack assessment | Production-Grade Gates, frontier workload, system economics, manufacturing continuity, multi-generation closure | separating real production substitution from autonomous frontier closure | inferring frontier closure from one domestic component or one benchmark |

The point of the report is therefore not to make every reader adopt the same conclusion. It is to make the **relevant denominator, mechanism, and reverse signal explicit before a decision is made**.

---

## 5. How to read the report

This chapter is the **entry point**, not a second full synthesis. Chapter 32 is the integrated Master View after the evidence and mechanisms have been developed.

Recommended paths:

- **Fastest decision path:** Ch01 → Ch32 → Ch30
- **Resource allocation / traditional end markets:** Ch03 → Ch04–Ch08 → Ch21 → Ch32
- **Platform and substitution competition:** Ch02 → Ch12–Ch17 → Ch32
- **Capital formation and clearing:** Ch19 → Ch22–Ch24 → Ch32
- **Method, monitoring, and falsification:** Ch27 → Ch29 → Ch30 → Ch32

Readers who need a number should follow that number to the thematic chapter and its source. Readers who need the full causal judgment should use Chapter 32.

---

## 6. Executive conclusion

The strongest current interpretation is not "AI wins and everything else loses," and it is not "more supply will solve the problem automatically."

It is:

> **AI/HPC is reprioritizing multiple layers of the infrastructure stack. The decisive variables are residual qualified supply, system-level substitution, bottleneck migration, power/LPS delivery, capital quality, and the ability to convert installed compute into productive workloads.**

That combination currently supports **S2 — Baseline Concentration**. The report should move away from S2 only when those underlying variables move.

# Part I · Chapter 2: NVIDIA's System Stack and Platform Power

## 1. NVIDIA's moat is a system-stack moat

NVIDIA's most important advantage is no longer the standalone performance of a single GPU generation. It is the ability to turn accelerators, HBM, scale-up fabric, compiler/runtime, libraries, rack architecture, and deployment tooling into a repeatable production system with low in-platform migration friction. The official GB200 NVL72 specification makes the shift in the commercial unit of delivery explicit:[^1]

**Table 2.1 — GB200 NVL72 rack-scale system structure**

| Layer | Official specification / structure |
|---|---|
| GPU | 72 Blackwell GPUs |
| CPU | 36 Grace CPUs |
| GPU memory | 13.4 TB HBM3E |
| CPU memory | 17 TB LPDDR5X |
| Scale-up domain | 72-GPU NVLink domain |
| Rack | liquid-cooled rack-scale system |

**Source:** NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 official product page.[^1]  
**Note:** The table reports the official system specification; it does not represent shipment volume, utilization, or customer deployment scale.

This changes how competition must be measured. In the add-in-card era, FLOPS, memory capacity, and card price could dominate the comparison. At rack scale, the comparison has to include memory hierarchy, scale-up/scale-out interconnect, compiler/runtime, distributed-training software, power/cooling, deployment tooling, and workload-migration cost.

A cheaper ASIC die therefore does not automatically imply a cheaper production AI system.

## 2. NVLink / NVSwitch internalizes scale-up communication

Frontier-model training is not limited by single-GPU compute alone. Tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, expert parallelism, and collective communication push performance toward bandwidth, topology, synchronization, and collective implementation.

The strategic value of NVLink/NVSwitch is that scale-up communication is designed as a platform-internal capability. GB200 NVL72 organizes 72 GPUs inside one NVLink domain; NVIDIA's current product page reports **130 TB/s of aggregate NVLink bandwidth per rack**.[^1]

That does not prove Ethernet-based alternatives are inherently incapable of substitution. It changes the substitution problem:

> A challenger must replace not one GPU, but the production capability created by **compute + memory + in-domain interconnect + the software execution model**.

For that reason, this report does not use unverified nanosecond-level latency comparisons or treat promotional benchmarks as independent measurements. The relevant evidence is production workload behavior: post-migration throughput, utilization, engineering cost, and reliability.

## 3. CUDA / PTX is a cross-generation software asset

CUDA's strategic value should not be reduced to an imaginary fixed "software tax" that does not appear in financial disclosures. It is better understood as a long-lived software asset:

- compiler and kernel ecosystem;
- libraries;
- profiling / debugging;
- framework integration;
- distributed communication;
- inference / training runtime;
- deployment tooling;
- developer knowledge.

PTX matters because it provides a relatively stable intermediate representation. Upper-layer software does not need to be rewritten from scratch every time the GPU generation changes. Hardware can move from Hopper to Blackwell to Rubin while a meaningful share of software assets remains reusable.

That creates a cross-generation mechanism:

**larger installed base → more production software assets → lower in-platform upgrade cost → higher out-of-platform migration cost.**

This is why NVIDIA's advantage cannot be measured by one benchmark or proved by an undisclosed "CUDA margin."

## 4. Rack-scale architecture extends switching cost into physical infrastructure

When the purchasing unit becomes the rack, migration costs extend from software into physical infrastructure. Customers build not only code, but also:

- rack / pod topology;
- power distribution;
- liquid cooling;
- networking;
- firmware;
- cluster management;
- scheduling and performance validation.

Changing one accelerator may be a procurement action. Changing a rack-scale system can require revalidating software-hardware coordination and data-center engineering.

This is where chip-only benchmarks most easily understate system power. The farther the system extends into racks, pods, and sites, the more challengers must prove deployment time, reliability, and total cost of ownership—not simply peak compute.

## 5. Platform profit can become next-generation reservation power

If system-level advantage produces high profit and free cash flow, it can influence the supply chain. The relevant company-level anchors are straightforward:

**Table 2.2 — NVIDIA seller-side economics and forward supply commitments**

| Metric | Current public value |
|---|---:|
| FY26 Data Center revenue | US$193.737B |
| FY26 NVIDIA-defined non-GAAP free cash flow | US$96.575B |
| FY27 Q2 revenue | US$96.221B |
| FY27 Q2 Data Center revenue | US$89.0B |
| FY27 Q2 GAAP gross margin | 75.0% |
| FY27 Q2 GAAP operating income | US$63.734B |
| 2026-07-26 manufacturing, supply, and capacity commitments | US$279B |

**Source:** NVIDIA FY26 results, FY27 Q2 results, and FY27 Q2 Form 10-Q.[^2][^3][^4]  
**Note:** US$279B is the aggregate manufacturing, supply, and capacity commitment; public filings do not provide a supplier-level split.

The FY27 Q2 10-Q states that the latest commitments are primarily associated with memory and manufacturing facilities required for data-center infrastructure systems.[^4] The filing does not split the US$279B across TSMC, CoWoS, SK hynix, Micron, Samsung, or any other individual supplier.

The number therefore demonstrates the scale of aggregate forward supply commitments; it is not evidence of any specific supplier's future revenue.

This creates a testable cross-generation reinforcing mechanism:

**high system profit → stronger supply commitments and resource reservation → greater delivery certainty → stronger customer retention → next-cycle system revenue.**

It is not an automatic monopoly formula. Suppliers still optimize for customer diversification, credit quality, utilization, geopolitics, and long-run bargaining balance.

## 6. System power has clear physical boundaries

NVIDIA does not directly manufacture every critical scarce layer. It still depends on:

- leading-edge foundries;
- HBM vendors;
- the advanced-packaging ecosystem;
- data-center operators;
- grid / power suppliers.

Strong platform power therefore does not make physical supply fully endogenous. A mismatch in TSMC capacity, HBM, advanced packaging, or power can constrain next-generation delivery.

This is why the report separates **Scarce-layer Value Capture** from a simple market-share monopoly framework. A system platform can have strong coordination and bidding power while remaining constrained by the supply elasticity of external physical layers.

## 7. The relevant competitive challenge is a second system stack

The strategic significance of Google TPU/Ironwood, AWS Trainium, Microsoft Maia, and Meta MTIA is not merely the existence of another chip.[^5] Hyperscalers also possess:

- captive large-scale workloads;
- cloud distribution;
- control of data-center infrastructure;
- internal compiler/runtime software;
- in-house interconnect and rack/pod design;
- the ability to optimize a narrower workload at system level.

The competitive frame is therefore not:

> NVIDIA GPU vs. custom ASIC

but:

> **NVIDIA system stack vs. cloud system stack**

That shift can produce two effects that pull in opposite directions and still coexist:

1. **Platform-profit diversion:** in-house cloud systems reduce dependence on part of NVIDIA's platform profit pool;
2. **Upstream resource competition:** those systems still compete for advanced logic, HBM, advanced packaging, and power.

Successful cloud custom silicon does not automatically relieve upstream physical scarcity.

## 7A. Reported Hugging Face transaction: platform power may extend from runtime into developer distribution

On August 27, 2026, Reuters, citing The Information, reported that NVIDIA had agreed to acquire Hugging Face for approximately **US$12.9B**.[^6] As of this report's evidence cutoff on **August 28, 2026**, this report had not obtained a formal NVIDIA or Hugging Face announcement confirming closing, final transaction conditions, or regulatory approval. It is therefore recorded as a **reported transaction**, not as a completed consolidation fact.

Hugging Face is strategically relevant because it is not merely a model-download website. Its official product surface spans the Hub, models, datasets, Spaces, Transformers, and inference/deployment products, connecting model discovery, asset distribution, tooling, evaluation, and deployment.[^7]

If the reported transaction ultimately closes, NVIDIA's platform boundary could extend from:

> **accelerator → CUDA/runtime → networking → rack/system**

toward:

> **accelerator → CUDA/runtime → model discovery/distribution → deployment path**

That creates a potential reinforcing loop:

**hardware installed base → CUDA/software assets → model/runtime optimization → developer default path → workload deployment → accelerator demand.**

This report treats it as a **developer-distribution / vertical-foreclosure risk** to monitor, not as a new load-bearing theory, and does not pre-label it as completed software monopoly.

The key question is not whether non-NVIDIA hardware remains technically present on Hugging Face. It is whether ownership changes lead to persistent and measurable bias in the platform's defaults:

- default model-page / benchmark emphasis toward NVIDIA runtimes;
- preferred inference / endpoint backends;
- ranking or visibility of NVIDIA-optimized artifacts, quantization paths, containers, or deployment flows;
- weakening first-class support for ROCm, XLA, CPU, or other accelerators;
- rising migration friction away from NVIDIA;
- stronger commercial incentives for model creators to publish NVIDIA-optimized variants first.

This risk is distinct from conventional CUDA lock-in. CUDA lock-in mainly operates after a workload has selected the NVIDIA execution environment. A distribution-layer foreclosure risk can emerge earlier:

> **model discovery → tool selection → runtime selection → deployment → accelerator.**

It can therefore move platform lock-in upstream into the developer funnel.

### 7A.1 Counter-boundaries

Even if the transaction closes, full software foreclosure would not automatically follow:

- open-weight models can be mirrored, self-hosted, or distributed across multiple registries;
- Hugging Face has historically operated as a multi-framework / multi-vendor ecosystem;
- model weights, open libraries, and alternative hubs preserve some portability;
- competitors can reduce single-point dependence through independent registries, runtimes, cloud distribution, and neutral-foundation governance.

The mechanism should gain weight only if **ranking, interoperability, deployment friction, and real workload distribution** change persistently.

## 8. Evidence standard for moat erosion

The NVIDIA system moat should not be judged from product-launch count or single-chip performance. The structure weakens only if several of the following variables move together:

- cloud system stacks reach production scale in frontier training / high-value inference;
- open software materially lowers CUDA migration cost;
- alternative scale-up fabrics reach production-grade scale;
- engineering cost and performance loss during multi-stack migration continue to fall;
- scarce upstream resources stop disproportionately supporting NVIDIA's roadmap;
- major customers distribute real workloads across multiple systems rather than running only benchmarks or narrow internal tests.

If several of these changes persist, NVIDIA's platform power could move from "system-level pricing power" toward a more negotiable "integration advantage." If migration remains expensive while in-platform generational upgrades stay low-friction, the system moat remains intact.

## 9. Current read

As of August 2026, the most accurate description is neither "GPU competition is over" nor "cloud ASICs have replaced NVIDIA."

It is:

> **NVIDIA currently has the most mature commercial general-purpose AI system stack; hyperscalers have built a real second system-stack path, but the extent of substitution must be validated through production workloads, migration cost, utilization, and upstream resource dependence.**

That is the starting point for the report's analysis of TSMC, HBM, advanced packaging, power, and the capital cycle. The competitive unit has moved from the die to the system, and the system remains constrained by multiple external scarce layers.

## 10. What would change the view

The judgment on NVIDIA's system-stack power should be downgraded if several signals persist together:

- frontier / high-value production workloads migrate at scale to other stacks;
- CUDA/runtime migration cost falls materially and is validated in production;
- alternative interconnect / rack systems achieve broad external adoption;
- NVIDIA supply commitments contract materially while competitors improve quantity assurance;
- seller-side margin / cash generation and installed-base retention deteriorate together.

A single custom-chip announcement, one-quarter market-share move, or theoretical benchmark advantage is not sufficient by itself to prove that the system-stack moat has failed.

# Part I · Chapter 3: AI Resource Reallocation and Non-AI Residual Capacity

## 1. The claim: priority can change before absolute shortage appears

AI does not need to “take all capacity” to change semiconductor and infrastructure economics. Reallocation starts at the margin.

The most exposed resources are those that are both **shared with AI/HPC demand and slow to expand**:

- advanced logic;
- HBM / selected DRAM;
- advanced packaging;
- high-end substrates / networking;
- selected power-management components;
- data-center power.

The report uses **resource reallocation pressure** as shorthand for this mechanism; it is not treated as a separate empirical law:

> **When AI/server workloads offer higher risk-adjusted returns, longer order duration, stronger payment certainty, and better expected utilization, constrained supply and the next unit of capital tend to move toward that demand.**

The analytical object is therefore the **opportunity cost of the next qualified unit of scarce capacity**, not a claim that AI physically consumes every semiconductor category.

---

## 2. Mechanism: the opportunity cost of the next scarce unit

Resource reallocation can be described as:

> **high-value AI/server demand → higher expected return → product-mix / capacity-allocation shift → lower residual capacity for lower-priority demand**

The mechanism requires several conditions:

- capacity cannot expand quickly in the short run;
- different end markets share a physical or capital pool;
- AI/server customers can offer longer orders, prepayments, or greater purchasing certainty;
- suppliers expect higher risk-adjusted returns from the higher-value demand.

The mechanism is therefore not simply “a higher price.” It is a repricing of the **opportunity cost of the next unit of scarce resource**.

---

## 3. Markets clear through allocation as well as price

During severe shortages, markets do not clear through spot price alone.

Long-term agreements, customer credit, prepayments, purchasing scale, and allocation fulfillment affect how much volume a buyer actually receives.

TrendForce stated in January 2026 that after U.S. CSPs locked in part of available capacity, other buyers had to accept higher prices to secure supply allocation. In March 2026, it also reported that PC OEMs and module makers with lower allocation-fulfillment rates had to obtain incremental supply at higher prices.[^1][^2]

Therefore:

> **willingness-to-pay ≠ guaranteed quantity**

Resource pressure must be separated into two variables:

1. **Price Pressure:** how much a buyer must pay for the same quantity;
2. **Quantity Assurance:** whether the buyer can obtain enough volume on schedule even if it accepts the price.

For traditional end markets, the second variable can matter more than short-term spot pricing.

---

## 4. Residual capacity is the downstream denominator

Effective supply available to traditional markets can be represented as:

```text
NonAI_Residual(t)
= Effective_Supply(t)
- AI_Server_Absorption(t)
- Other_Priority_Demand(t)
```

This resolves a common analytical error:

> **Growth in total supply does not imply equal growth in supply available to traditional end markets.**

If total effective supply expands but AI/server absorption expands faster, Non-AI Residual Capacity can still decline.

Evaluating whether smartphones, PCs, general servers, automotive, or industrial markets are returning to looser conditions therefore requires more than tracking:

- global wafer capacity;
- global DRAM bit growth;
- global packaging capacity;
- global power-project pipelines.

The relevant question is **how much effective residual supply those end markets can obtain within the same quality, qualification, generation, and delivery window**.

---

## 5. Reallocation changes capital formation, not just current supply

The long-run effect of resource reallocation extends beyond current allocation into the next round of capital formation.

The AI Infrastructure Economy and Traditional Device Economy share parts of the same advanced-logic, memory, packaging, and power-management resource base, but they differ in:

- willingness to pay;
- contract duration;
- prepayment structure;
- utilization visibility;
- BOM sensitivity;
- end-market price elasticity.

Suppliers are therefore deciding not only “who receives more capacity today,” but also:

> **which product class offers the higher risk-adjusted return on the next dollar of CapEx.**

The report uses **two-speed semiconductor economics** as shorthand for that divergence.

It is not a claim that consumer electronics are permanently sacrificed. It means **AI/HPC is gaining greater influence over marginal semiconductor capital formation**.

---

## 6. Memory is the cleanest observed transmission path

Micron disclosed that, under **same technology node / same number of bits** conditions, HBM3E requires approximately **3× the wafer supply of DDR5**.[^3]

TrendForce forecasts HBM + RDIMM at approximately **51% of 2026 DRAM bit supply**.[^4]

Together, these two anchors show:

> **The manufacturing-resource intensity of high-value AI/server memory can exceed what bit share alone implies.**

The memory-layer transmission mechanism is therefore:

> HBM / server-memory demand rises → wafer / cleanroom / capital tilts toward higher-value products → conventional DDR/LPDDR residual supply changes → price / configuration / quantity-assurance pressure reaches traditional end markets

The boundaries remain important:

- 3× is a same-node / same-bits wafer-supply trade ratio;
- 51% (2026E) includes HBM + RDIMM;
- 51% is a 2026E forecast;
- neither figure can be rewritten as HBM wafer share.

---

## 7. Logic and packaging must remain separate denominators

TSMC's 2025 smartphone platform represented **29%** of annual net revenue, while HPC represented **58%**.[^5]

That establishes HPC as the largest revenue platform, but these are revenue-mix measures—not customer-level wafer allocation.

Leading-edge logic and advanced packaging must also remain separate:

- logic wafer availability does not guarantee a complete system can be delivered;
- packaging tightness does not imply equal customer allocation;
- customer revenue share cannot be converted into wafer share or CoWoS share.

Resource reallocation therefore cannot be summarized by one synthetic “AI share of global capacity.” It is a set of allocation shifts across different layers with different physical units.

---

## 8. Transmission depends on overlap, supply elasticity, and buyer power

Transmission into traditional markets depends on three conditions.

### Shared-resource overlap

The more an end market shares physical inputs with AI, the higher its exposure.

### Supply elasticity

The harder the resource is to expand quickly, the stronger the short-run pressure.

### Buyer bargaining power

Buyers with LTAs, purchasing scale, inventory, strong balance sheets, and end-market pricing power can absorb or delay the shock more effectively.

These end systems should not be placed into one universal “AI took the chips” funnel.

**Table 3.1 — Layered exposure of non-AI / Physical-AI end systems**

| End system | Main shared or adjacent upstream layers | Main transmission path | What can be inferred | What must not be inferred |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Smartphone / PC | selected leading-edge SoC/GPU, LPDDR/DRAM, NAND, selected packaging | BOM, configuration, upgrade tax, replacement cycle, quantity assurance | opportunity cost of shared resources can rise | industry disappearance; a named customer losing a known wafer quantity |
| Game console | custom SoC/APU, GDDR/DRAM, NAND/SSD, selected packaging/test | BOM, promotion, hardware margin, long-generation cost-down, quantity assurance | memory procurement can affect hardware volume, promotion, and profit cadence | direct HBM competition; known wafers taken by AI; next generation must be delayed or repriced |
| Router / broadband | consumer DRAM/NAND, low bargaining power | higher price + weaker allocation | weaker buyers can face price and quantity pressure together | all end markets rise by the same multiple |
| Automotive / industrial / production lines | mature memory, MCU/analog, power, selected ADAS compute, packaging/test | lead time, qualification, EOL/part number, supply continuity | long qualification and long lifecycles reduce rapid substitution; adjacent product-mix shifts can matter | automotive electronics are directly “consumed” by GPU/HBM demand |
| Robotics / Physical AI | industrial control + sensors/actuation + edge accelerator + cloud retraining | industrial-electronics and edge-AI constraints can stack | robots can be exposed to both industrial and AI-compute pools | every robot needs frontier HBM; factories stop because AI took GPUs |
| Avionics / radar / space electronics | trusted/qualified logic, RF/power, rad-hard/rad-tolerant parts, special packaging/test | small-volume line economics, qualification, trusted access, long-lifecycle support | commercial high-volume markets can weaken small-volume special-demand bargaining power | aircraft, radar, or satellites are directly stopped by HBM shortage |
| Naval / other long-life defense systems | long-life qualified electronics, power/communications, trusted supply, maintenance spares | EOL, supplier longevity, small-volume economics | long-lived systems need sustained part-number and trusted-supply continuity | naval platforms “need NVIDIA capacity” |

**Source:** Chapter 21 smartphone / PC / game-console / consumer / industrial transmission evidence; NXP / ST automotive-longevity disclosures; U.S. GAO / DMEA trusted-microelectronics evidence; NASA/JPL space-radiation assurance materials.[^6][^7][^8][^9][^10]  
**Note:** The AI-era transmission strength differs substantially across the later rows. For defense / aerospace / space, the public evidence primarily establishes the structural weakness of low-volume, special, long-life, trusted supply in a commercial market; it does **not** establish AI/HPC as the direct cause of a specific program's cost or delay.

The key boundary is:

> **Resource Gravity is selective. The closer an end system is to shared advanced logic / memory / packaging, the more direct the transmission. The more it depends on trusted, long-life, RF/power, rad-hard, or special-process capacity, the more likely the channel runs through capital, equipment, engineering capacity, and supplier economics.**

Detailed transmission into pricing, configuration, replacement cycles, and observed examples belongs in [Chapter 21](part-III-ch21-consumer-transmission.md).

---

## 9. Reallocation is conditional, not a one-way law

Resource reallocation contains a self-correcting mechanism.

If AI/HBM demand absorbs enough supply to drive up conventional DRAM, other logic-product, or traditional-component pricing, the per-unit resource economics of non-AI products improve.

That can produce:

> **AI allocation rises → non-AI residual supply tightens → non-AI price / margin rises → supplier rebalancing incentive strengthens**

Likewise, if AI workload monetization weakens, utilization falls, or supply elasticity improves rapidly, AI Resource Gravity can weaken.

It is therefore not a permanent law that “AI always drains every resource.” It is a **dynamic capital-allocation mechanism**.

---

## 10. Observable signs of strengthening or weakening

Signals of **strengthening** include:

- larger AI/server forward commitments;
- HBM / advanced-packaging tightness persisting across generations;
- supplier product mix continuing to tilt toward high-value AI/server products;
- declining Non-AI Residual Capacity;
- widening gaps in quantity assurance;
- incremental CapEx becoming more explicitly centered on AI/HPC.

Signals of **weakening** include:

- materially higher supply elasticity;
- stronger traditional-product economics inducing supplier rebalancing;
- sustained reductions in HBM / packaging lead times;
- improved allocation fulfillment;
- weaker AI utilization / monetization;
- forward commitments being reduced or delayed.

---

## 11. Current read

As of August 2026, public evidence is more consistent with:

> **AI Resource Gravity materially affecting selected shared scarce layers and changing the resource environment for traditional end markets through Non-AI Residual Capacity and quantity assurance.**

The process remains selective and dynamic, and it is subject to price feedback, supply expansion, and substitution.

The most accurate formulation is therefore not “AI is taking every chip.” It is:

> **AI is raising the opportunity cost of selected critical resources and changing how suppliers rank incremental capacity, product mix, and priority customers.**

# Part I · Chapter 4: Advanced Logic Allocation — TSMC, N2, and the Next Unit of Qualified Capacity

## 1. The unit of analysis is qualified incremental capacity

Leading-edge logic is necessary but not sufficient for frontier AI. The relevant variable is not “who has access to an advanced node?” but **who can secure qualified incremental capacity at the required volume and timing while HBM, packaging, interconnect, power, and software are ready to convert that wafer output into a production system**.

The relevant advanced-manufacturing question is therefore:

> **Who can repeatedly secure enough qualified N2/N2P/A16-class capacity, on schedule, without another layer becoming the binding constraint?**

A rumored wafer price does not answer that question. Volume, qualification, delivery timing, roadmap continuity, and cross-layer readiness do.

## 2. TSMC baseline: capacity, node mix, platform mix

**Table 4.1 — TSMC 2025 capacity, technology, and platform-revenue structure**

| Metric | 2025 |
|---|---:|
| 12-inch-equivalent wafer shipments | ~15.0M |
| annual capacity | >17M |
| 3 nm wafer-revenue share | 24% |
| 5 nm | 36% |
| 7 nm | 14% |
| ≤7 nm | 74% |
| HPC platform | 58% of net revenue; +48% YoY platform growth |
| Smartphone platform | 29%; +11% YoY platform growth |
| largest / second-largest customer | 19% / 17% of annual revenue |

**Source:** TSMC 2025 Annual Report, 2025 Form 20-F, and 4Q25 Presentation.[^1][^2][^3]  
**Note:** Platform share and node share are revenue-based metrics. Customer revenue share cannot be converted into wafer, node, or CoWoS allocation.

These figures show that HPC became TSMC's largest platform while TSMC continued to serve a broad customer base. They do not support the claim that TSMC has become a dedicated fab for any one customer.

## 2A. 2Q26: HPC remains a major marginal driver of advanced-manufacturing capital

TSMC's official 2Q26 results provide a current cross-section:[^8]

- HPC platform revenue mix: **66%**;
- smartphone: **22%**;
- advanced technologies at 7 nm and below: **77% of wafer revenue**;
- 2026 capital budget: **US$60B–64B**.

These remain revenue-mix and company-CapEx measures, not AI wafer allocation.

They support a narrower conclusion:

> **HPC has become one of the central marginal demand drivers of TSMC's advanced-manufacturing capital formation, while the company continues to raise investment in advanced processes and advanced packaging.**

This strengthens the report's focus on the destination of the next capital dollar, but it does not support claims that:

- 66% of wafers are AI;
- 77% of advanced-technology revenue belongs to NVIDIA;
- all US$60–64B of CapEx is AI-specific;
- smartphones have lost leading-edge access.

## 3. Revenue share is not an allocation denominator

The 2025 largest-customer share of 19% and second-largest-customer share of 17% are **annual-revenue ranking disclosures**.[^2]

They cannot be converted into N2 wafer share, 3 nm wafer share, CoWoS share, HPC wafer share, or physical wafer counts.

A different anonymized customer table supports year-over-year comparison: Customer A **12%→19%** and Customer B **22%→17%** from 2024 to 2025.[^4] The annual largest/second-largest ranking and the anonymized A/B series answer different questions and cannot be combined into a fictional longitudinal trajectory for one customer.

Likewise, HPC at 58% is a platform revenue share, not a wafer-shipment share.

## 4. N2 matters through launch access, scale, and continuity

N2 matters for more than transistor density. Competitors care about:

- timing of volume production;
- available scale;
- yield / delivery stability;
- HBM and packaging support;
- system-level performance conversion;
- roadmap continuity.

Access to a node does not automatically create a system victory. If memory, packaging, interconnect, or power are missing, complete-system delivery remains constrained.

## 5. Scarce-capacity access remains layer-specific

The report does not use one cross-layer percentage to summarize access to advanced logic, HBM, packaging, networking, and power.

Those are different physical pools and must be evaluated separately.

The relevant questions are:

- how many qualified suppliers exist;
- whether buyers receive planned quantities on time;
- lead time and allocation fulfillment;
- long-term agreements / prepayments;
- delivery schedules;
- buyer credit quality;
- supply elasticity.

If reliable customer-level allocation data becomes available for one physical layer, a percentage can be used for that layer. It cannot be extended into a full-stack "resource capture share."

## 6. Allocation is multi-variable, not rank-deterministic

Advanced-capacity allocation is more likely to reflect a combination of price, committed volume, contract duration, prepayment, credit quality, utilization certainty, roadmap stability, customer diversification, and geopolitical risk.

The deterministic claim that "the number-one customer gets all the best resources" is therefore not supportable.

A more defensible mechanism is that order scale, credit, prepayment, and roadmap certainty increase a buyer's bargaining power over incremental resources, while suppliers retain incentives to diversify customers, protect long-run bargaining power, and manage geopolitical risk.

## 7. Packaging is a separate physical pool

TSMC first-party material confirms advanced-packaging tightness, but customer-level CoWoS allocation is not disclosed.[^5] TrendForce's estimate that NVIDIA represented more than 60% of 2025 CoWoS demand is B-grade institutional evidence.[^6]

No report-side packaging-geometry ratio is used in the formal analysis to infer rack output or customer allocation. Front-end logic wafers and back-end advanced-packaging capacity are different physical pools and cannot be divided into one another.

This is why "leading-edge logic available" and "complete AI system deliverable" are different questions.

## 8. Foundry share is not frontier-system substitution

TrendForce estimates 1Q26 foundry revenue shares at roughly **72% for TSMC**, **6.5% for Samsung Foundry (excluding System LSI)**, and **5.1% for SMIC**.[^7]

These are revenue shares, not frontier-AI capacity shares. A second supply system capable of substitution must also prove node performance, yield, advanced packaging, the HBM ecosystem, customer qualification, and software/system integration.

"Another foundry exists" and "a complete second frontier-AI supply stack exists" are therefore different propositions.

## 9. Current read

TSMC's strategic position rests on three conditions that currently coexist: strong leading-edge logic, HPC as its largest platform, and advanced packaging as a publicly confirmed growth constraint.

The key forward variables are not one quarter's customer revenue shares, but who can secure incremental N2/N2P/A16-class capacity, how HBM and packaging supply evolve, how cloud custom silicon competes for new capacity, and whether a second manufacturing system can deliver a credible logic + packaging + memory alternative.

## 10. What would change the view

Signals that should reduce TSMC's leading-edge strategic leverage include:

- a second foundry achieving independently verifiable, large-scale external production at the same-generation node;
- customer qualification, yield, delivery, and advanced packaging combining into a real substitute;
- N2/N2P/A16 supply elasticity improving materially faster than demand growth;
- advanced-packaging constraints disappearing on a sustained basis;
- leading-edge workloads migrating materially toward another manufacturing system.

Higher foundry revenue share alone, a single technology demonstration, or policy subsidies are not sufficient to establish an equivalent frontier-manufacturing second source.

# Part I · Chapter 5: HBM Economics — Manufacturing Intensity, Residual Capacity, and Memory Scarcity

## 1. The memory question is manufacturing intensity, not bit demand alone

HBM should not be treated as just another GPU BOM line. In frontier systems it affects model capacity, batching, context length, concurrency, communication, and accelerator utilization; at rack scale, its manufacturing intensity becomes a system-level capacity constraint.

The industrial question is therefore not simply "how many HBM bits are demanded?" It is:

> **How much wafer input, cleanroom space, packaging capacity, qualification effort, and capital does each unit of high-value memory absorb, and what residual supply remains for conventional DRAM?**

That is why HBM can reprice the broader memory system even when aggregate DRAM bit capacity continues to grow.

## 2. Micron's ~3× disclosure is the first-party manufacturing anchor

Micron's FY24 Q2 prepared remarks provide a clear boundary: at the **same technology node and for the same number of bits**, HBM3E requires approximately **3× the wafer supply of DDR5**.[^2] Micron's FY25 10-K further confirms that producing the same number of HBM bits requires more wafers and cleanroom space.[^3]

This evidence supports the following conclusions:

- HBM3E consumes more manufacturing input per bit than DDR5;
- HBM expansion places greater pressure on DRAM wafer / cleanroom input;
- effective residual capacity for conventional DRAM can face stronger pressure.

It does **not** mean that HBM is priced at 3× DDR5, nor can it be treated as an immutable "3:1 law" for every fab and every HBM generation. Micron's public statement on HBM4 is only that the trade ratio is expected to rise further; a specific HBM4/HBM4E ratio still requires future vendor disclosure.

## 3. The 51% forecast uses a different denominator

TrendForce **forecasts** that **HBM + RDIMM together will account for roughly 51% of 2026 DRAM bit supply**.[^4] This B-grade institutional forecast must retain three boundaries:

1. the 51% includes **HBM and RDIMM** and cannot be rewritten as "51% of DRAM is HBM";
2. it is a **bit-supply** share, not a wafer share;
3. it is a **2026E forecast**, not completed full-year actuals.

Combined with Micron's same-bit wafer trade ratio, this creates a more important mechanism: **bit share does not fully capture manufacturing-input pressure.** When a high-value bit requires more wafer and cleanroom input, its impact on manufacturing resources can exceed its share of bits.

## 4. Residual capacity is the downstream denominator

Memory reallocation can be expressed as a clear transmission chain:

**AI/server memory demand rises → HBM/RDIMM mix rises → wafer / cleanroom / packaging input shifts toward high-value products → conventional DDR/LPDDR residual capacity tightens → non-AI end markets face greater price and configuration pressure.**

The key variable is not total global DRAM capacity. It is the effective supply actually left for consumer electronics and other traditional workloads after AI/server demand has absorbed the priority resources.

This is why the report uses **Non-AI Residual Capacity** as the central memory metric rather than treating gross DRAM-capacity growth as proof that traditional markets have returned to abundance.

## 5. HBM has changed memory-vendor economics

SK hynix reported FY25 revenue of **KRW97.1467T**, operating profit of **KRW47.2063T**, operating margin of **49%**, and net income of **KRW42.9479T**, while stating that HBM revenue more than doubled year over year.[^5]

These figures do not prove that HBM alone generated all profit, but they are sufficient to show that high-value memory product mix has materially improved memory-vendor economics. Conventional server memory remains important as well, reinforcing the point that HBM and DDR5/RDIMM are not fully isolated capital and manufacturing systems.

## 6. Supply is concentrated; the public denominator is incomplete

High-end HBM supply is concentrated primarily among SK hynix, Samsung, and Micron. The barriers are not just DRAM-fab CapEx. They also include:

- TSV / stacking;
- yield learning;
- advanced-packaging integration;
- customer qualification;
- generation timing;
- high-volume manufacturing stability.

Public first-party material is insufficient to construct a fully comparable and auditable three-vendor HBM market-share table. This report therefore does not upgrade media or sell-side estimates into company-official share data.

### 6.1 Price feedback limits one-way scarcity narratives

Resource reallocation contains a price-feedback mechanism. TrendForce's June 2, 2026 model estimate found that after conventional DRAM prices rose sharply from the second half of 2025, **DDR5 64GB RDIMM per-wafer revenue exceeded HBM in 1Q26**; the same research estimated HBM profitability below that of DDR5 64GB RDIMM.[^6]

This is B-grade institutional estimation, not product-level realized gross-margin disclosure from Samsung, SK hynix, or Micron. Its analytical value is the self-correcting mechanism it reveals:

> HBM/AI demand rises → conventional-DRAM residual supply tightens → DDR5/RDIMM prices rise → conventional-DRAM per-wafer economics improve → the relative incentive for further HBM conversion declines → memory vendors rebalance product mix.

Resource reallocation is therefore not an infinitely one-way process. Long-run allocation depends on risk-adjusted return per scarce manufacturing input, qualification, yield, generation transitions, and customer-contract structure.

## 7. Rack specs show intensity, not industry demand

GB200 NVL72's **13.4 TB of HBM3E per rack** is a useful system-level material identity.[^1]

It shows that once procurement moves from an accelerator card to a rack-scale system, memory intensity must also be evaluated at the system level.

But without a public rack shipment or deployment count, the specification cannot be scaled into an industry PB-demand estimate.

Therefore:

> **Per-system HBM specifications can describe memory intensity; industry demand still requires observed shipments, customer demand, or memory-vendor supply data.**

## 8. HBM4 raises cross-layer capital density without a fixed public multiplier

The complexity of next-generation HBM comes not only from higher stack counts. It can also involve logic base dies, advanced foundry processes, packaging, testing, and qualification.

If logic base dies use more advanced processes, the memory bottleneck extends further into foundry and packaging:

**HBM vendor → logic base die → advanced foundry → advanced packaging → accelerator qualification**

HBM can therefore evolve from a "memory bottleneck" into a system bottleneck spanning memory, foundry, and packaging. Before vendors formally disclose the data, however, HBM3E's ~3× ratio cannot be mechanically rewritten as 4× or 5× for HBM4, and one 12-Hi or 16-Hi configuration cannot be treated as the universal HBM4 production standard.

## 9. HBM does not clear like a standard commodity-memory cycle

One important difference between HBM and standard commodity memory is generation-specific qualification. Product generations move quickly, they are closely tied to accelerator generations, qualification cycles are long, and obsolescence risk is higher.

The industry can therefore experience:

> **looser supply in an older HBM generation while the next frontier generation remains constrained.**

Oversupply in one generation does not automatically solve qualification, yield, and packaging constraints in the next.

## 10. Inference can shift the bottleneck without eliminating memory economics

Some inference workloads can trade bandwidth for lower-cost DDR/LPDDR, but frontier inference still faces KV-cache, long-context, large-batch, MoE-routing, low-latency serving, and multi-accelerator communication constraints.

More importantly, RDIMM is already included in TrendForce's forward AI/server memory structure. Shifting some workloads from HBM toward DDR5 therefore changes the cost/bandwidth tradeoff inside a broader shared memory-resource pool rather than creating an independent supply base.

## 11. Current read and falsification

HBM scarcity is not inevitable. The current mechanism would weaken materially if:

- memory architecture sharply reduces dependence on high-bandwidth stacked memory;
- algorithmic efficiency persistently lowers memory bandwidth / capacity demand;
- the HBM wafer/cleanroom trade ratio improves materially;
- stacking, yield, logic-base, and advanced-packaging supply elasticity rises sharply;
- conventional DRAM and HBM manufacturing resources become much more decoupled.

The long-run claim is not that "HBM will always be scarce." It is:

> **As long as frontier-system bandwidth demand grows faster than HBM supply elasticity and manufacturing input per bit remains materially above conventional DRAM, HBM will remain a core scarce layer of AI infrastructure.**

## References

[^1]: NVIDIA, “GB200 NVL72,” official product page, https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/gb200-nvl72/
[^2]: Micron Technology, FY24 Q2 Prepared Remarks, 2024-03-20, HBM3E ≈3× DDR5 wafer supply at same node / same bits, https://s25.q4cdn.com/621799436/files/doc_financials/2024/q2/FY24-Q2-Prepared-Remarks.pdf
[^3]: Micron Technology, FY25 Form 10-K, HBM wafer and cleanroom requirements, U.S. SEC, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/723125/000072312525000028/mu-20250828.htm
[^4]: TrendForce, 2026-08-25, 2026E HBM + RDIMM share of DRAM bit supply, https://www.trendforce.com/presscenter/news/20260825-13198.html
[^5]: SK hynix, FY25 Financial Results, https://news.skhynix.com/en/sk-hynix-announces-fy25-financial-results/
[^6]: TrendForce, 2026-06-02, per-wafer revenue comparison for HBM and DDR5 64GB RDIMM, https://www.trendforce.com/presscenter/news/20260602-13074.html

# Part I · Chapter 6: Advanced Packaging — The Quantity Gate Between Wafers and Deliverable Systems

## 1. Packaging is the quantity gate between wafers and systems

A frontier accelerator is not commercially deliverable when the logic die leaves the fab. Multi-die integration, HBM, interposers, substrates, testing, yield, and qualification still have to close within the same delivery window.

Advanced packaging therefore acts as a **quantity gate**:

> **front-end logic available ≠ complete AI system deliverable**

The relevant industrial variable is not only how many leading-edge wafers can be fabricated, but how many qualified systems can pass through the packaging/integration layer in the same delivery window.

## 2. Tightness is first-party observable; revenue labels still need denominator discipline

TSMC's public statements are sufficient to establish advanced-packaging tightness:[^1][^2]

- 4Q24: management described relevant capacity as **very tight** and unable to satisfy all customer demand;
- 2Q26: management stated more directly that packaging capacity was **so tight that now it limits my customers' growth**.

Revenue disclosures must retain their original year-specific labels:

- 4Q24 transcript: **advanced packaging and testing >8% of revenue**;
- 4Q25 transcript, using the company's corrected wording: **advanced packaging slightly over 10% of 2025 revenue**.[^5]

These labels are not perfectly identical. This report therefore does **not** treat >8% → >10% as a strict same-denominator time series, nor does it rewrite the 2025 "advanced packaging" figure back into "advanced packaging + testing."

## 3. Tightness is observable; customer allocation is not

TSMC public material supports the following: advanced packaging is tight, CoWoS is an important part of that system, and packaging tightness is limiting customer growth.

TSMC does not disclose an auditable customer-level CoWoS allocation table for this report, nor does it provide an official CoWoS share by customer.

Two questions therefore have to remain separate:

- **A-grade fact:** packaging / CoWoS tightness;
- **not disclosed:** exactly how much CoWoS capacity each customer receives.

Annual customer revenue share, wafer revenue share, and CoWoS customer share are not interchangeable.

## 4. Demand concentration is observable only through institutional estimates

TrendForce's research on 2025 CoWoS demand identifies NVIDIA as the largest demand customer and estimates its demand share at **more than 60%**.[^3]

The evidence grade must remain **B — institutional estimate**. The figure is useful for analyzing demand concentration and designing stress tests, but it cannot be rewritten as:

- TSMC officially confirming that NVIDIA received >60% of allocation;
- >60% being a 2026 actual;
- NVIDIA possessing exclusive CoWoS rights.

The correct use is: **highly concentrated demand has a real institutional anchor, while actual allocation still awaits first-party disclosure.**

## 5. Packaging is a separate physical denominator

The formal report does not use a report-side "CoWoS wafers per rack" geometry factor to infer industry rack capacity.

Advanced-packaging capacity depends on packaging flow, interposer/substrate constraints, HBM integration, tool capacity, testing, yield, and qualification. It is not interchangeable with TSMC's front-end 12-inch-equivalent wafer shipments.

Therefore:

- front-end logic wafers cannot be divided by a packaging-geometry factor to infer rack output;
- packaging demand share cannot be converted into customer allocation;
- rack specifications cannot be converted into actual shipments without observed deployment data.

## 6. Packaging can bind before front-end logic

Leading-edge logic supply can grow through new fabs, process migration, and capacity expansion. Advanced packaging simultaneously depends on tools, interposers, substrates, testing, process flows, HBM integration, and qualification.

The result is:

> **logic wafer available ≠ system deliverable**

Advanced nodes are closer to an entry ticket into a frontier system; advanced packaging can become the quantity gate that determines how many complete systems are delivered. Both matter, but their physical units and expansion clocks are different.

## 7. Incremental access must be measured at the packaging layer

The forward question is not a synthetic cross-layer capture ratio.

It is whether competing buyers can obtain qualified advanced-packaging supply with acceptable:

- lead time;
- allocation fulfillment;
- delivery stability;
- supplier diversification;
- generation transition;
- integration yield.

That evidence should be evaluated directly at the packaging layer.

## 8. Second stacks do not automatically escape packaging / HBM

Google, AWS, Microsoft, and Meta custom accelerator systems can divert part of NVIDIA's platform profit, but their next-generation systems still rely heavily on advanced logic, HBM, and high-density integration.

Two effects can therefore coexist:

1. **platform substitution:** in-house cloud systems reduce dependence on the full NVIDIA platform;
2. **upstream competition:** those same systems increase demand for the same advanced manufacturing, HBM, and packaging resources.

More custom silicon does not automatically mean lower CoWoS/HBM pressure.

## 9. Bottleneck location and profit location are different questions

Advanced packaging can be the system-delivery bottleneck without having the highest margin in the value chain. TSMC management stated in 2Q24 that advanced-packaging gross margin had historically been significantly below corporate average and was approaching, but had not yet reached, the company average.[^4]

Physical bottlenecks and profit pools therefore have to remain separate:

- packaging may determine **whether the system can be delivered**;
- the system platform can still capture stronger economics through software, interconnect, integration, and customer switching costs.

> **bottleneck location ≠ profit location**

This distinction is essential for AI-infrastructure value-capture analysis.

## 10. Packaging is an independent China-closure gate

A frontier AI parallel stack cannot be judged from logic nodes alone. Even if accelerator dies can be produced, insufficient advanced packaging, substrates, HBM integration, testing, or high-volume yield can still prevent stable delivery of large systems.

"Domestic chip production" therefore cannot hide packaging as an independent physical layer. China system closure must validate logic, HBM, packaging, interconnect, software, and power separately.

## 11. Current read and falsification

As of August 2026, the most defensible conclusions are:

- TSMC has confirmed advanced-packaging tightness with first-party evidence;
- TrendForce provides a B-grade institutional anchor for highly concentrated NVIDIA CoWoS demand;
- customer-level allocation remains undisclosed by TSMC;
- 5.37 wafers/rack is only a D-grade geometry stress test;
- custom silicon can still compete for the same upstream scarce resources.

The judgment that advanced packaging is a core scarce layer should be weakened if TSMC stops describing packaging as a growth constraint, lead times fall materially, customer-level allocation becomes more distributed, and HBM/packaging supply elasticity continues to improve.

# Part I · Chapter 7: Time-to-Power — From Rack Density to Deployable AI Capacity

## 1. The power question is deployable capacity, not electricity price

At roughly **120 kW/rack**, power is no longer just an operating-cost input. It becomes a deployment gate.[^1]

A D-grade stress conversion makes the scale visible:

> 500 racks × 120 kW/rack = **60 MW of rack-level full-load power**

This does not describe any specific campus and excludes facility overhead. It shows why hundreds of dense racks quickly pull **powered land, interconnection, substations, transformers, cooling, firm generation, and permitting** into the same delivery chain as chips and HBM.

The relevant industrial variable is therefore:

> **Time-to-Power: how long it takes to move from project intent to energized, usable capacity for a real AI workload.**

## 2. Power requires a delivery-state model

Power / LPS projects should be separated into six states:

> **Announced → Contracted / Secured → Permitted → Construction / Transition → Energized → Utilized**

A 1 GW PPA cannot be rewritten as "1 GW of AI compute online." A secured LPS position or future IT-GW design capacity cannot be treated as energized load, and a 500 MW development target cannot be converted directly into an active rack count. The real economic value of a project depends on how far it has advanced from announcement toward high-utilization delivery—not on the maximum MW/GW in a headline.

Generation MW/GW, PPA capacity, IT-GW, energized facility load, and utilized AI load must retain their distinct physical identities.

## 3. Representative projects sit on different delivery clocks

### 3.1 Microsoft / Constellation: restarting an existing ~835 MW nuclear asset

Microsoft and Constellation entered a **20-year PPA** supporting the restart of the former Three Mile Island Unit 1 as the Crane Clean Energy Center, with an approximately **835 MW** public capacity anchor.[^2]

The case shows how hyperscaler demand can support a large existing power asset returning to service.

But 835 MW is a project / unit-capacity anchor, not evidence that 835 MW is already being delivered in real time to AI data centers. The project still sits on regulatory, repair, restart, interconnection, and commercial-operation clocks.

Constellation's official release states that the restart requires significant investment but does **not** disclose a US$1.6B restart CapEx figure. That number therefore does not enter this chapter's fact layer.

### 3.2 Talen / AWS: a revised PPA of up to 1,920 MW

The Talen/AWS revised PPA has a full contract quantity of **up to 1,920 MW** and runs through 2042.[^3]

Talen's 2026 Q2 10-Q states that the transition to the revised AWS PPA **occurred in April 2026**. An earlier 2025 10-K had stated that **full transition was expected in spring 2027**.[^3][^4]

April 2026 can therefore be used as the current disclosed status of the revised-PPA transition. It **cannot** be interpreted as proof that every physical conversion, transmission modification, and full-delivery step had already been completed.

The relevant forward indicators are the capacity ramp, energized MW, AWS load, and utilization.

This case shows that regulation and commercial structure can change the delivery path for power without making large-scale AI electricity demand disappear.

### 3.3 Google / Kairos: 50 MWe in 2030 and up to 500 MWe by 2035

The Google/Kairos public timeline is much longer: **Hermes 2 up to 50 MWe in 2030**, followed by a fleet of **up to 500 MWe by 2035**.[^5]

This is better understood as a long-duration supply option, industrial-learning path, and capacity hedge than as spot power that can be called on in 2026–2028.

The near-term value of SMRs therefore lies mainly in future optionality; they should not be used to erase today's interconnection, transformer, and powered-site constraints.

### 3.4 PORTS-Pike / NVIDIA / SB Energy / OpenAI: secured LPS with initial 4.25 IT-GW design capacity

On **August 17, 2026**, NVIDIA disclosed a different infrastructure structure at the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus: NVIDIA is providing credit support for land, power, and shell buildout with SB Energy; the initial deployment is designed to support **4.25 IT-GW**; OpenAI will use the site; and SB Energy will build, own, and operate the data center.[^7]

Planned capacity is expected to come online in phases beginning in **2028**.

This makes secured LPS a more direct precursor to deployable compute than a generic headline PPA. But **4.25 IT-GW is still design / planned capacity, not 2026 energized or utilized AI load**.

## 4. Project capacities cannot be summed into active AI load

The project numbers above do not share one physical identity. Generation MW/MWe, PPA capacity, and IT-GW design capacity sit at different layers and cannot be added into one active AI-load figure.

**Table 7.1 — Representative AI power / LPS pathways**

| Project | Nominal scale | Primary status |
|---|---:|---|
| Crane / Microsoft | ~835 MW | restart + regulatory process |
| Talen / AWS | up to 1,920 MW | revised-PPA transition / ramp |
| Kairos / Google | 50 MWe in 2030; up to 500 MWe by 2035 | long-duration development |
| PORTS-Pike / NVIDIA / SB Energy / OpenAI | initial 4.25 IT-GW design capacity | LPS secured / future phased buildout from 2028 |

**Source:** Constellation, Talen Energy, Kairos Power / Google, and NVIDIA.[^2][^3][^4][^5][^7]  
**Note:** Generation MW/MWe, PPA capacity, and IT-GW design capacity are different physical quantities. Their contract, permitting, construction, energization, and utilization states must remain separate.

These pathways represent different infrastructure mechanisms: restarting an existing large generator, restructuring a large-load PPA, developing next-generation nuclear supply, and securing land + power + shell for future AI-factory buildout. Their maturity, units, clocks, and utilization dates are not directly comparable.

## 5. Grid queues measure friction, not AI demand

Berkeley Lab's Queued Up data show that active U.S. generation/storage interconnection requests peaked near **2,600 GW at the end of 2023** and stood at approximately **2,061 GW at the end of 2025**.[^6]

These numbers cannot be converted into "the United States lacks 2,061 GW of data-center power." The queue is primarily generation/storage projects and includes projects that may withdraw, duplicate one another, or experience long delays.

The narrower supported conclusion is that **interconnection and transmission buildout can take years, making Time-to-Power a real constraint.**

What matters for AI system delivery is how many MW a specific region can actually deliver inside a specific hardware-generation window—not the total GW sitting in a national queue.

### 5A. Grid delivery has an equipment-procurement clock

Time-to-Power is also constrained by the supply chain of the grid itself. The IEA reports that new transmission lines can take **four to eight years** in advanced economies, while procurement wait times for critical grid components have lengthened materially.[^8] A separate IEA transmission-supply-chain review reports typical procurement of **two to three years for cables** and **up to four years for large power transformers**, with average lead times for both almost doubling since 2021.[^9]

### Table 7.2 — Grid delivery frictions relevant to Time-to-Power

| Constraint | Public institutional anchor | Correct interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| New transmission | 4–8 years in advanced economies | broad grid-build clock; not a project-specific AI-data-center lead time |
| Cables | 2–3 years procurement | component-supply constraint inside transmission / interconnection delivery |
| Large power transformers | up to 4 years procurement | equipment bottleneck that can delay substation / grid delivery |
| Interconnection queue | multi-year studies and high withdrawal rates | friction indicator; not a direct measure of unmet AI demand |

**Source:** IEA and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.[^6][^8][^9]  
**Note:** These are grid-system and equipment-supply anchors, not a claim that every AI campus faces the same lead time. They strengthen the narrower conclusion that energized capacity is constrained by **permitting + interconnection + equipment procurement + construction**, not by generation nameplate alone.

This also sharpens the delivery-state boundary: a project can have land, a PPA, and a financing plan while still lacking a timely transformer, cable, substation, or grid-connection path.

## 6. Time-to-Power is a system-competition variable

Advanced chips can advance on monthly and quarterly product clocks. Power infrastructure often advances on multi-year clocks.

That creates a variable comparable in importance to the chip roadmap:

> **Time-to-Power**

Projects with existing grid interconnection, powered land, substation / transformer capacity, firm generation, and executable permitting paths gain a timing advantage.

Hyperscaler competition is therefore not only about who acquires more accelerators. It is also about an **illustrative deployment-scale question**:

> **who can energize the next 50 MW / 100 MW / 500 MW of systems sooner.**

The 50 / 100 / 500 MW values are scenario-scale markers used to illustrate Time-to-Power; they are not disclosed project capacities.

## 7. Power can become binding after semiconductor supply eases

AI infrastructure does not have one permanent bottleneck.

One possible **Rolling Bottleneck Cascade** is:

> HBM / advanced packaging tight → hardware delivery constrained → manufacturing supply expands → more racks reach sites → power / interconnection becomes binding → deployment and utilization slow → next-cycle hardware orders / commitments decelerate

The reverse is also possible. If power infrastructure is built far ahead of workload demand, the problem can shift from scarcity to low utilization and weak capital returns.

"Power is now a core constraint" and "power is not yet the sole dominant bottleneck" can therefore both be true.

## 8. Power contracts and compute assets run on different clocks

AI servers have shorter technological and economic lives than major power assets and long-duration PPAs.

Crane involves a **20-year PPA**, while compute hardware will turn over much faster.[^2] This creates a classic duration mismatch:

> **shorter-cycle compute asset vs. longer-cycle power / infrastructure asset**

In high-demand scenarios, long-duration power access can be a moat. In S4 Capital Hard Landing, the same long-duration obligation can become a burden.

Power contracts therefore need to be evaluated through duration, ramp, take-or-pay / cancellation terms, project execution, utilization, and residual value.

## 9. When does power become the binding constraint?

Power should be upgraded from "one of the core constraints" to "the dominant constraint" only if several signals appear together:

- major buyers repeatedly disclose power/interconnection as the binding growth ceiling;
- delivered hardware sits idle waiting to be energized;
- energized capacity persistently lags deployment plans;
- next-generation orders are delayed by power constraints;
- Time-to-Power remains a decisive differentiator for high-value powered sites;
- utilization and capital returns deteriorate systematically because of power-delivery timing.

As of August 2026, public evidence supports a narrower conclusion:

> **Power has joined HBM and advanced packaging as a core physical constraint, but the evidence is not yet sufficient to show that power alone dominates the entire AI-infrastructure expansion rate.**

## 10. What would change the view

The judgment that power / LPS is a core AI-infrastructure constraint should be downgraded if the following conditions persist:

- Time-to-Power shortens materially;
- secured / contracted projects convert into energized capacity at high and predictable rates;
- transformers, substations, grid interconnection, and cooling stop causing major deployment delays;
- energized capacity grows persistently faster than deployable compute demand;
- regional power price / availability stops materially affecting site selection.

Headline GW growth alone is not sufficient evidence that the power bottleneck has disappeared. The relevant test is the speed of state transition into energized capacity and actual utilization.

## References

[^1]: NVIDIA, DGX GB200 Hardware Guide, rack power approximately 120 kW, https://docs.nvidia.com/dgx/dgxgb200-user-guide/hardware.html
[^2]: Constellation, Crane Clean Energy Center / Microsoft 20-year PPA and approximately 835 MW unit, https://investors.constellationenergy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/constellation-launch-crane-clean-energy-center-restoring-jobs
[^3]: Talen Energy, 2026 Q2 Form 10-Q, revised AWS PPA transition and up to 1,920 MW, U.S. SEC, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1622536/000162253626000066/tln-20260630.htm
[^4]: Talen Energy, 2025 Form 10-K, expected full transition timing, U.S. SEC, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1622536/000162253626000017/tln-20251231.htm
[^5]: Kairos Power / Google partnership, Hermes 2 up to 50 MWe in 2030 and fleet up to 500 MWe by 2035, https://www.kairospower.com/google
[^6]: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, “Queued Up” 2026 update, active interconnection queue, https://emp.lbl.gov/news/backlog-power-plants-seeking-transmission-grid-connection-eased-somewhat-2025-amidst
[^7]: NVIDIA, “NVIDIA Guarantees SB Energy's PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio to Exclusively Host NVIDIA AI Compute,” 2026-08-17, https://investor.nvidia.com/news/press-release-details/2026/NVIDIA-Guarantees-SB-Energys-PORTS-Pike-Technology-Campus-in-Ohio-to-Exclusively-Host-NVIDIA-AI-Compute/default.aspx

[^8]: International Energy Agency, “Energy and AI — Executive summary,” grid-connection queues, transmission lead times, and critical-component delays, https://www.iea.org/reports/energy-and-ai/executive-summary
